citation.title: Conservative Variance Estimation for Sampling Designs with Zero Pairwise Inclusion Probabilities

standing_assumptions:
The work is a short theory paper (Survey Methodology, June 2013, Vol. 39, No. 1, printed pp. 231–241; the article is PDF pp. 3–13 of the staged main.pdf) with two propositions and three corollaries, each with a printed proof, and an official simulation supplement (staged/supplements/smj_suppl.pdf, printed pp. A1–A10) that the article points to on p. 239. Everything below was read from the rendered page images (the staged pages, and the staged PDFs re-rendered at 220 dpi when this list was fixed).
[Population and design: Section 2, first paragraph, pp. 232–233 (PDF pp. 4–5)] “Consider a population $U$ indexed by $1, \ldots, k, \ldots N$ and a sampling design such that the probability of inclusion in the sample for unit $k$ is $\pi_k$, and the joint inclusion probability for units $k$ and $l$ is $\pi_{kl}$. Under a measurable design, there are two conditions: (1) $\pi_k > 0$ and $\pi_k$ is known for all $k \in U$ and (2) $\pi_{kl} > 0$ and $\pi_{kl}$ is known for all $k, l \in U$. Non-measurable designs include those for which either of the two conditions for a measurable design do not hold. Failure to meet the former condition precludes unbiased estimation of totals.”
[Estimator of the total and inclusion indicators: p. 233 (PDF p. 5)] “The Horvitz-Thompson estimator of a population total is $\hat t = \sum_{k \in s} y_k/\pi_k = \sum_{k \in U} I_k\, y_k/\pi_k$, where $I_k \in \{0, 1\}$ is unit $k$'s inclusion indicator, the only stochastic component of the expression, with $\mathrm{E}(I_k) = \pi_k$, the inclusion probability, and $s$ and $U$ refer to the sample and the population, respectively. Define $\mathrm{E}(I_k I_l) = \pi_{kl}$, which is the probability that both units $k$ and $l$ from $U$ are included in the sample. Since $I_k I_k = I_k$, $\mathrm{E}(I_k I_k) = \pi_{kk} = \pi_k$ by construction. When condition 1 holds, as we assume throughout, the Horvitz-Thompson estimator is unbiased.”
[Variance and its estimator under measurability: Section 2.1, p. 233 (PDF p. 5)] “By Horvitz and Thompson (1952), the variance of the Horvitz-Thompson estimator for the total is $$\mathrm{Var}(\hat t) = \sum_{k \in U}\sum_{l \in U}\mathrm{Cov}(I_k, I_l)\frac{y_k}{\pi_k}\frac{y_l}{\pi_l} = \sum_{k \in U}\mathrm{Var}(I_k)\left(\frac{y_k}{\pi_k}\right)^2 + \sum_{k \in U}\sum_{l \in U\backslash k}\mathrm{Cov}(I_k, I_l)\frac{y_k}{\pi_k}\frac{y_l}{\pi_l}.$$ We label a sample from a measurable design, $s^M$, and an unbiased estimator for $\mathrm{Var}(\hat t)$ on $s^M$ is $$\widehat{\mathrm{Var}}(\hat t) = \sum_{k \in s^M}\sum_{l \in s^M}\frac{\mathrm{Cov}(I_k, I_l)}{\pi_{kl}}\frac{y_k}{\pi_k}\frac{y_l}{\pi_l} = \sum_{k \in U}\sum_{l \in U} I_k I_l\frac{\mathrm{Cov}(I_k, I_l)}{\pi_{kl}}\frac{y_k}{\pi_k}\frac{y_l}{\pi_l},$$ where the only stochastic part of the expression is $I_k I_l$, and unbiasedness is by $\mathrm{E}(I_k I_l) = \pi_{kl}$.”
[Non-measurable designs, the term $A$ and the sample $s^0$: Section 2.2, pp. 233–234 (PDF pp. 5–6)] “We now examine the case where condition 2 does not hold: $\pi_{kl} = 0$ for some units $k, l \in U$. Because $I_k$ is a Bernoulli random variable with probability $\pi_k$, $\mathrm{Cov}(I_k, I_l) = \pi_{kl} - \pi_k\pi_l$ for $k \ne l$, and $\mathrm{Cov}(I_k, I_k) = \mathrm{Var}(I_k) = \pi_k(1 - \pi_k)$. Then, we can re-express the variance above as, $$\mathrm{Var}(\hat t) = \sum_{k \in U}\pi_k(1 - \pi_k)\left(\frac{y_k}{\pi_k}\right)^2 + \sum_{k \in U}\sum_{l \in U\backslash k}(\pi_{kl} - \pi_k\pi_l)\frac{y_k}{\pi_k}\frac{y_l}{\pi_l}$$ $$= \sum_{k \in U}\pi_k(1 - \pi_k)\left(\frac{y_k}{\pi_k}\right)^2 + \sum_{k \in U}\sum_{l \in \{U\backslash k:\pi_{kl} > 0\}}(\pi_{kl} - \pi_k\pi_l)\frac{y_k}{\pi_k}\frac{y_l}{\pi_l} - \underbrace{\sum_{k \in U}\sum_{l \in \{U\backslash k:\pi_{kl} = 0\}} y_k y_l}_{A}.$$ For $k$ and $l$ such that $\pi_{kl} = 0$, the sampling design will never permit unbiased estimation of the component of the variance labeled as $A$ above, since we will never observe $y_k$ and $y_l$ together. We label a sample from a design where condition 2 fails as $s^0$. When $\widehat{\mathrm{Var}}(\hat t)$ is applied to $s^0$, the result is unbiased for $\mathrm{Var}(\hat t) + A$.” On the page the underbrace spans the double sum $\sum_k\sum_l y_k y_l$ only, not the minus sign before it, so $A = \sum_{k \in U}\sum_{l \in \{U\backslash k:\pi_{kl} = 0\}} y_k y_l$; Proposition 1 (p. 234) and the display of $A$ at the head of p. 239 (PDF p. 11) agree with this.
[Conventions that every statement inherits] The outcomes $y_1, \ldots, y_N$ are fixed real numbers; expectation, variance and covariance are over the sampling design alone (‘the only stochastic component’ is $I_k$). Condition 1 ($\pi_k > 0$ for every $k$) is assumed throughout; ‘known’ plays no part in any mathematical statement. A double sum $\sum_{k \in U}\sum_{l \in \{U\backslash k:\pi_{kl} = 0\}}$ runs over ordered pairs $(k, l)$ of distinct units with $\pi_{kl} = 0$, so each unordered pair is counted twice; $\sum_{k \in U}\sum_{l \in \{U:\pi_{kl} > 0\}}$ includes the diagonal $l = k$ (as $\pi_{kk} = \pi_k > 0$). On a sample $s^0$ the estimator $\widehat{\mathrm{Var}}(\hat t)$ is the sum over pairs of sampled units, which the proof of Proposition 1 (p. 234) writes as $\sum_{k \in U}\sum_{l \in \{U:\pi_{kl} > 0\}} I_k I_l\frac{\mathrm{Cov}(I_k, I_l)}{\pi_{kl}}\frac{y_k}{\pi_k}\frac{y_l}{\pi_l}$.
[What the paper does not print] No probability space is displayed: a sampling design is a probability distribution on the subsets $s \subseteq U$, with $I_k = 1$ exactly when $k \in s$. The paper does not say that $U$ is finite and non-empty other than through the indexing $1, \ldots, N$. In Section 3 the exponents $a_{kl}, b_{kl}$ are indexed by ordered pairs and are not required to be symmetric in $(k, l)$; $1/a_{kl} + 1/b_{kl} = 1$ with both positive forces $a_{kl}, b_{kl} > 1$; $|y|^{a}$ is the real power of a nonnegative number (so $|0|^{a} = 0$).
[Supplement, Section A, p. A1 (supplement PDF p. 1)] “In the simulations, expected values of $\widehat{\mathrm{Var}}(\hat t)$ and $\widehat{\mathrm{Var}}_C(\hat t)$ were computed exactly using expressions from Propositions 1 and 2 in the main text. Expected values for alternative estimators were computed using exact expressions for bias when available and via simulated sample draws otherwise. All simulations study expected values of estimators for the sampling variance of the Horvitz-Thompson estimator for the population mean, $$\hat\mu_{HT} \equiv \frac{1}{N}\hat t.$$” So in the supplement the estimand is $\mathrm{Var}(\hat\mu_{HT}) = \mathrm{Var}(\hat t)/N^2$ and the estimators are $(1/N^2)\widehat{\mathrm{Var}}(\hat t)$ and $(1/N^2)\widehat{\mathrm{Var}}_{C2}(\hat t)$; by Proposition 1 the bias of $(1/N^2)\widehat{\mathrm{Var}}(\hat t)$ is $A/N^2$.
[Supplement, Section B, one unit per stratum: pp. A1–A2 (supplement PDF pp. 1–2)] “Simplifying that context, we consider two strata each of size $M$, in which case $N = 2M$. From each stratum a single unit is randomly sampled. Thus, for unit $k$ in stratum $s$, $$\pi_{ks} = \pi = \frac{1}{M},$$ and for units $k$ and $l$ in strata 1 or 2, we have $$\pi_{ks,lt} = \begin{cases} 0 & \text{if } s = t \\ \frac{1}{M^2} & \text{if } s \neq t \end{cases}.$$ In stratum $s$, outcomes $y_s = (y_{1s}, ..., y_{Ms})$ are drawn as, $$y_{ks} = \alpha_s + \epsilon_{is},$$ where $\alpha_s$ is a stratum-specific constant and $\epsilon_{ks} \sim \mathrm{N}(0, 1)$. For the two strata, 1 and 2, we keep things simple by setting $\alpha_1 = \alpha = -\alpha_2$, in which case the intra-class correlation over strata is given by, $$\rho_{ICC} = \frac{\alpha^2}{\alpha^2 + 1/2}.$$ We simulated 1,000 sets of outcomes, $(y_1, y_2)$ over varying values of $M$ and $\rho_{ICC}$. To each set, we applied the single-unit-per-stratum design. Then, we computed three approximations of the sampling variance of the Horvitz-Thompson estimator of the population mean: 1. The Horvitz-Thompson estimator for the sampling variance of the estimator for the population mean, $(1/N^2)\widehat{\mathrm{Var}}(\hat t)$. 2. The bias-adjusted estimator, $(1/N^2)\widehat{\mathrm{Var}}_{C2}(\hat t)$. 3. The “collapsed stratum” estimator (Wolter, 2007, 51-2), which for this case, given unit $k$ from stratum 1 and unit $l$ from stratum 2 selected into $s^0$, equals, $$\widehat V_{CS}(\hat\mu_{HT}) = \frac{1}{N^2}\left(\frac{y_{k1}}{\pi_1} - \frac{y_{l2}}{\pi_2}\right)^2 = \frac{1}{4}(y_{k1} - y_{l2})^2.$$” (The two misprints in these displays, the missing restriction to distinct units and $\epsilon_{is}$ for $\epsilon_{ks}$, are finding P027-E006; see P027-T18.) The supplement does not say that the errors $\epsilon_{ks}$ are independent, or that the two strata are sampled independently; both are the ordinary reading and are used by the validators.
[Supplement, Section C, systematic PPS sampling: pp. A3–A4 (supplement PDF pp. 3–4)] “For the simulations, a size variable, $x = (x_1, ..., x_N)$, is produced as a vector of $N$ random draws from a negative binomial distribution with mean 6, variance 16, and offset of 1 to avoid zero values. These settings were meant to recreate a data scenario roughly comparable to Wolter (2007, Ch. 8). An outcome variable, $y$, is created as, $$y_k = \beta x_k + \epsilon_k,$$ for $k = 1, ..., N$, where $\beta = \rho(\sigma_y/\sigma_x)$, $\epsilon_k$ is Gaussian noise with mean zero and standard deviation $\sigma_y\sqrt{1 - \rho^2}$, and $\sigma_x$ and $\sigma_y$ are the standard deviation of the $N$ values in $x$ and $y$ respectively, where $\mathrm{E}_x(\sigma_x) = 4$ and we fix $\sigma_y = 30$ (again, to mimic data distributed as in Wolter (2007, Ch. 8)). Thus, $x$ and $y$ have a linear relationship through the origin and their correlation is given by $\rho$. Systematic PPS sampling was implemented such that each unit's first order inclusion probability is given by, $$\pi_k = \frac{x_k}{\sum_{l=1}^{N} x_l}m,$$ where $m$ is the size of the systematic sample, and joint inclusion probabilities are computed as per Madow (1949).” The with-replacement estimator (p. A3): $$\widehat{\mathrm{Var}}_{WR}(\hat\mu_{HT}) = \frac{1}{N^2 m(m - 1)}\sum_{k \in s^0}\left(\frac{y_k}{p_k} - \hat t\right)^2,$$ “where $p_k = \pi_k/m$ is the notional “per-draw” selection probability.” The periodic design (pp. A3–A4): “we performed a second set of simulations where the size variable, $x$, was drawn as an $N$-length vector of repeating 2's and 10's, thus maintaining variance values that are comparable to the previous simulation. Also, so that we could provide an illustration of the performance of $\widehat{\mathrm{Var}}_{C2}(\hat t)$, we produced $y_k$ values in the same manner as above, but then worked with the demeaned value, $$\tilde y_k \equiv y_k - \bar y,$$ as the variable with which $\hat\mu_{HT}$ was computed.” The supplement does not display the systematic selection rule; the validators and the targets below use the usual cumulative-size rule with one uniform random start (unit $k$ occupies the interval $[c_{k-1}, c_k)$ with $c_k = \sum_{a \le k} x_a$; with $I = \sum_l x_l/m$ and $u$ uniform on $[0, I)$ the sample is the set of units whose intervals contain $u, u + I, \ldots, u + (m-1)I$), and the order $x = (2, 10, 2, 10, \ldots)$. The $(N, m)$ pairs of Tables A2 and A3 (pp. A7–A8) are $(8, 2), (40, 2), (120, 30), (600, 30), (240, 60), (1200, 60)$, so $q = N/m \in \{4, 20\}$.

canonical_claim.name_in_paper: Supplement Section C and Table A3 (the $\widehat{\mathrm{Var}}_{C2}$ results for the periodic design), corrected by the disclosure that the estimator was applied to the original units; formal content: the unit-level and the totalled $\widehat{\mathrm{Var}}_{C2}$ in the periodic design
canonical_claim.location: Supplement p. A4 (staged/supplements/smj_suppl.pdf, PDF p. 4), discussion of Table A3 and Figure A3; Table A3 on supplement p. A8 (PDF p. 8); Figure A3 on supplement p. A10 (PDF p. 10); main p. 237 (PDF p. 9)
canonical_claim.statement:
Sol's repair (validated.json, P027-N005, smallest_repair), verbatim: "Add to the periodic simulation discussion and Table A3/Figure A3 notes: 'The C2 results here apply the formula to the original units without combining always-co-selected units as recommended on main-text p. 237; they illustrate the uncombined-unit estimator.' If the intended comparison is instead the recommended procedure, replace its C2 results with combined-unit calculations and revise the discussion, retaining the original N^2 divisor for the population mean."
Mathematical content, with every hypothesis (validator's derivation.md, sections 2–5, 7 and 8).
Setting. As in P027-T2: $N = mC$ with $C = N/m \ge 2$ even ($C \in \{4, 20\}$ in Table A3), sizes $x_k = 2$ ($k$ odd), $10$ ($k$ even), systematic PPS sampling by cumulative sizes with one uniform start, and outcomes $z$ with $\sum_k z_k = 0$. The possible samples are $G_c = \{c, c + C, \ldots, c + (m-1)C\}$, $c = 1, \ldots, C$, with probabilities $p_c = 1/(3C)$ ($c$ odd), $5/(3C)$ ($c$ even). Write $Y_c = \sum_{k \in G_c} z_k$, $Q_c = \sum_{k \in G_c} z_k^2$, $S = \sum_c Y_c^2$, $Q = \sum_c Q_c$.
(i) [The possible samples are clusters.] For $k, l$ in the same $G_c$, $I_k = I_l$ on every sample, so $\Pr(I_k \ne I_l) = 0$; units in different sets are never selected together; the sets $G_c$ are the maximal sets of always-co-selected units. So the instruction of p. 237 applies to every unit of this design, and the totalled population has $C$ units with outcomes $Y_c$, exactly one of which is drawn, unit $c$ with probability $p_c$.
(ii) [Unchanged by totalling.] On the draw of $G_c$: $\hat t = Y_c/p_c$ and $\widehat{\mathrm{Var}}(\hat t) = (1 - p_c)Y_c^2/p_c^2$, for the original and for the totalled units alike. $V := \mathrm{Var}(\hat t) = \sum_c Y_c^2/p_c$ and $H := \mathrm{E}[\widehat{\mathrm{Var}}(\hat t)] = V - S$.
(iii) [Unit-level correction.] Each unit has exactly $N - m$ units with which its joint inclusion probability is zero. On the draw of $G_c$ the second double sum of $\widehat{\mathrm{Var}}_{C2}(\hat t)$ (p. 237) equals $(N - m)Q_c/p_c$; its expectation is $A^* = (N - m)Q$; so the unit-level estimator has $$U := \mathrm{E}\big[\widehat{\mathrm{Var}}_{C2}(\hat t)\big]_{\text{original units}} = V - S + (N - m)Q.$$
(iv) [Totalled correction.] Each cluster has $C - 1$ clusters with which its joint inclusion probability is zero. On the draw of cluster $c$ the second double sum equals $(C - 1)Y_c^2/p_c$; its expectation is $(C - 1)S$; so the totalled estimator has $$G := \mathrm{E}\big[\widehat{\mathrm{Var}}_{C2}(\hat t)\big]_{\text{totalled units}} = V + (C - 2)S.$$
(v) [The unit-level estimator is the larger, sample by sample.] On the draw of $G_c$, $$\widehat{\mathrm{Var}}_{C2}(\hat t)_{\text{original}} - \widehat{\mathrm{Var}}_{C2}(\hat t)_{\text{totalled}} = \frac{C - 1}{p_c}\big(mQ_c - Y_c^2\big) = \frac{m(C - 1)}{p_c}\sum_{k \in G_c}\Big(z_k - \frac{Y_c}{m}\Big)^2 \ge 0,$$ and $U - G = (C - 1)(mQ - S) \ge 0$. Both are conservative: $G - V = (C - 2)S \ge 0$.
(vi) [Bounds for the totalled estimator.] $\tfrac{3C}{5}S \le V \le 3CS$; hence, if $V > 0$, $$\frac{C - 2}{3C} \le \frac{G - V}{V} \le \frac{5(C - 2)}{3C}$$ ($[1/6, 5/6]$ for $C = 4$; $[3/10, 3/2]$ for $C = 20$).
(vii) [Outcome-averaged ratio.] Under the second-moment outcome model of P027-T2 (v) (constant $\beta$; errors with mean zero, common variance and zero covariances), $\mathrm{E}_y(Y_c^2)$ is the same number $L$ for every $c$, $\mathrm{E}_y(S) = CL$, $\mathrm{E}_y(V) = \tfrac{9C}{5}\mathrm{E}_y(S)$, and when $L > 0$ $$\frac{\mathrm{E}_y(G) - \mathrm{E}_y(V)}{\mathrm{E}_y(V)} = \frac{5}{9}\Big(1 - \frac{2}{C}\Big),$$ that is $5/18$ for $C = 4$ and $1/2$ for $C = 20$, for every $\rho$. This is a ratio of outcome-averaged quantities and not an identity for each population: for $N = 8$, $m = 2$, $z = (1, 0, -1, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0)$ one has $S = 2$, $V = 24$, $G = 28$ and $(G - V)/V = 1/6$.
On the mean scale every quantity is divided by the original $N^2$ (not by $C^2$).
Corrected claim: the $\widehat{\mathrm{Var}}_{C2}$ columns of Table A3 and the curve of Figure A3 are for the estimator applied to the original units ((iii)); the estimator the main text prescribes for this design is the totalled one ((iv)), whose relative bias obeys (vi).
canonical_claim.definitions_needed: $\widehat{\mathrm{Var}}_{C2}(\hat t)$ and the paragraph on clusters: main p. 237 (PDF p. 9), P027-T23 and P027-T8. $A$, $A^*$, $\hat t$, $\widehat{\mathrm{Var}}(\hat t)$: main pp. 233–236, standing assumptions and P027-T21. The periodic design and the demeaned outcomes: supplement pp. A3–A4, standing assumptions; the samples $G_c$ and their probabilities: P027-T2 (i). $\hat\mu_{HT} \equiv \hat t/N$: supplement p. A1. Not in the paper: the selection rule, the order of the sizes, and any statement of whether the reported $\widehat{\mathrm{Var}}_{C2}$ was computed before or after totalling.
canonical_claim.note: Repair cost recorded by Sol: none (a sentence of disclosure; no assumption or estimand changes). Not established (Sol): that the printed entries are correct for the unit-level estimator (no code or populations are staged; see P027-T19 for the four high-$\rho$ rows), or any mean-squared-error ranking. (ii) and (iii) give $U - H = (N - m)Q$, the identity $C - H = (N - m)\sum_i z_i^2/N^2$ of finding P027-N004 on the mean scale. The equal group sizes make (v) the equal-size case of P027-T4 (vi); the argument does not extend to unequal cluster sizes or to other exponents.

canonical_claim.name_in_paper: Supplement Section C: ‘Because $y$ is proportional to $x$ with $x \ge 1$, Proposition 1 in the main text indicates that the Horvitz-Thompson variance estimator for $\hat\mu_{HT}$, $(1/N^2)\widehat{\mathrm{Var}}(\hat t)$, provides a conservative approximation of the sampling variance of $\hat\mu_{HT}$’; the witness is the validator's construction and is not in the paper
canonical_claim.location: Supplement p. A3 (staged/supplements/smj_suppl.pdf, PDF p. 3), Section C, paragraph beginning ‘Because $y$ is proportional to $x$’; the outcome model $y_k = \beta x_k + \epsilon_k$ is displayed on the same page
canonical_claim.statement:
Exact witness (validator's construction; not in the paper): a population of the random-size simulation's model, with every size at least 1, for which the Horvitz-Thompson variance estimator is biased downward.
Population and design. $N = 8$, $m = 2$ (the first configuration of Table A2). Sizes $x = (1, 3, 1, 3, 1, 3, 1, 3)$ (positive integers, so in the support of the offset negative binomial law; $\sum_l x_l = 16$; $m\max_k x_k = 6 \le 16$). Outcomes $y^0 = (1, -1, 1, -1, 1, -1, 1, -1)$ (of the form $\beta x_k + \epsilon_k$ for any $\beta$, with $\epsilon_k = y^0_k - \beta x_k$). Systematic PPS sampling: unit $k$ occupies $[c_{k-1}, c_k)$, that is $[0,1), [1,4), [4,5), [5,8), [8,9), [9,12), [12,13), [13,16)$; $u$ is uniform on $[0, 8)$ and the sample consists of the units whose intervals contain $u$ and $u + 8$.
Claims.
(C1) [The design.] The possible samples are $\{1,5\}$ (probability $1/8$), $\{2,6\}$ ($3/8$), $\{3,7\}$ ($1/8$), $\{4,8\}$ ($3/8$). Hence $\pi_k = x_k/8 = m x_k/\sum_l x_l$ (the printed formula), $\pi_{kl} = \pi_k$ for $l \in \{k, k \pm 4\}$ and $\pi_{kl} = 0$ for the other 48 ordered pairs of distinct units.
(C2) [Sample by sample.] $\hat t = 16$ on $\{1,5\}$ and $\{3,7\}$ and $-16/3$ on $\{2,6\}$ and $\{4,8\}$; $\widehat{\mathrm{Var}}(\hat t) = 224$ and $160/9$ respectively.
(C3) [Expectations.] $\mathrm{E}(\hat t) = 0$; $\mathrm{Var}(\hat t) = 256/3$; $\mathrm{E}[\widehat{\mathrm{Var}}(\hat t)] = 208/3$; $A = -16$. On the mean scale: $\mathrm{Var}(\hat\mu_{HT}) = 4/3$, $\mathrm{E}[(1/N^2)\widehat{\mathrm{Var}}(\hat t)] = 13/12$, bias $-1/4 < 0$. So for this population, with $x \ge 1$ throughout, the estimator is not conservative.
(C4) [A neighbourhood.] For every $y$ with $|y_i - y^0_i| < 1/8$ for all $i$ (same $x$ and design), $A(y) \le -13/4 < 0$.
(C5) [What survives.] $A^* = 48$ and $\mathrm{E}[\widehat{\mathrm{Var}}_{C2}(\hat t)] = 352/3 \ge 256/3$.
What the witness contradicts: the inference from $x \ge 1$ and the outcome model to a nonnegative bias for each generated population. The realized $y$ of the model is not proportional to $x$ and need not be of one sign, so the same-sign condition of main p. 234 need not hold.
canonical_claim.definitions_needed: $A$, Proposition 1 and the sign remark after it (‘If the $y_k, y_l$ values are always nonnegative (or always nonpositive), then the bias is always nonnegative’): main p. 234 (PDF p. 6), P027-T20. $\hat\mu_{HT}$, the size law, $y_k = \beta x_k + \epsilon_k$, $\pi_k = m x_k/\sum_l x_l$: supplement pp. A1 and A3, standing assumptions. ‘Conservative’: nonnegative bias, $\mathrm{E}[(1/N^2)\widehat{\mathrm{Var}}(\hat t)] \ge \mathrm{Var}(\hat\mu_{HT})$, for the fixed population (main p. 235: ‘an expected value greater than or equal to the true variance ..., and is thus conservative’). $\widehat{\mathrm{Var}}_{C2}$: main p. 237. The selection rule is not displayed in the supplement (standing assumptions).
canonical_claim.note: P027-E003 is rated an error, Minor. Sol's verdict is confirmed, evidence type exact_counterexample, upheld on re-run. (C4) is what makes the failure an event of positive probability under independent Gaussian noise with positive variance (every listed $\rho < 1$): the box $|\epsilon_i - (y^0_i - \beta x_i)| < 1/8$ has positive probability (derivation.md, section 5; at $\rho = 1/20$, $\sigma_y = 30$ and the divisor-$N$ $\sigma_x = 1$, $\beta = 3/2$). The positive population-averaged biases of Table A2 are not called into question (P027-T11).

canonical_claim.name_in_paper: Supplement Section C, the sentence ‘Because $y$ is proportional to $x$ with $x \ge 1$, Proposition 1 ... provides a conservative approximation’, corrected: nonnegative bias after averaging over the generated outcomes
canonical_claim.location: Supplement p. A3 (staged/supplements/smj_suppl.pdf, PDF p. 3), Section C, paragraph beginning ‘Because $y$ is proportional to $x$’
canonical_claim.statement:
Sol's repair (validated.json, P027-E003, smallest_repair), verbatim: "Replace the sentence with: 'Conditional on the size vector x, the model has E_epsilon[y_k|x]=beta x_k and independent mean-zero errors. Proposition 1 therefore implies nonnegative HT variance-estimator bias after averaging over generated outcomes: E_epsilon[A|x]=beta^2 sum_{k != l: pi_kl=0} x_k x_l >= 0. It does not guarantee conservativeness for each realized finite population.' Interpret the Figure A2 label 'Conservative (HT)' as referring to that outcome average."
Mathematical content, with every hypothesis (validator's derivation.md, sections 2 and 6).
Setting. Fixed sizes $x_1, \ldots, x_N$ with $x_k \ge 1$ (positivity is all that is used). A sampling design on $U = \{1, \ldots, N\}$ that depends on $x$ only, with $\pi_k > 0$ for all $k$; $Z = \{(k, l) : k \ne l,\ \pi_{kl} = 0\}$. A real constant $\beta$ (in the supplement $\beta = \rho\,\sigma_y/\sigma_x$ is a function of $x$). Outcomes $y_k = \beta x_k + \epsilon_k$, where $\epsilon_1, \ldots, \epsilon_N$ are random variables with $\mathrm{E}_\epsilon(\epsilon_k) = 0$, finite variances and $\mathrm{E}_\epsilon(\epsilon_k\epsilon_l) = 0$ for $k \ne l$ (independent mean-zero Gaussian errors in the supplement). $\mathrm{E}_s$ and $\mathrm{Var}_s$ are over the sample with $(x, y)$ fixed; $\mathrm{E}_\epsilon$ is over the errors with $x$ fixed. $A(y) = \sum_{(k,l) \in Z} y_k y_l$.
(i) For $k \ne l$: $\mathrm{E}_\epsilon(y_k y_l) = \beta^2 x_k x_l$.
(ii) $$\mathrm{E}_\epsilon\big[A(y)\big] = \beta^2\sum_{k \ne l:\ \pi_{kl} = 0} x_k x_l \ \ge\ 0.$$
(iii) By Proposition 1 for each fixed $y$, $$\mathrm{E}_\epsilon\Big[\mathrm{E}_s\big[(1/N^2)\widehat{\mathrm{Var}}(\hat t)\big] - \mathrm{Var}_s(\hat\mu_{HT})\Big] = \frac{\beta^2}{N^2}\sum_{k \ne l:\ \pi_{kl} = 0} x_k x_l \ \ge\ 0:$$ the Horvitz-Thompson variance estimator is conservative on average over the generated outcomes.
(iv) This does not give $A(y) \ge 0$ for each realized $y$: in the design of P027-T10, $\sum_{(k,l) \in Z} x_k x_l = 176$, so $\mathrm{E}_\epsilon[A] = 176\beta^2$ ($= 396$ at $\beta = 3/2$), while $A(y^0) = -16$.
A guarantee for each population needs $A(y) \ge 0$, for example outcomes all of one sign (main p. 234), which the Gaussian errors do not ensure.
canonical_claim.definitions_needed: $A$, $\hat t$, $\widehat{\mathrm{Var}}(\hat t)$, Proposition 1: main pp. 233–234 (PDF pp. 5–6), standing assumptions and P027-T20. $\hat\mu_{HT} \equiv \hat t/N$, the size law, $y_k = \beta x_k + \epsilon_k$, $\beta = \rho(\sigma_y/\sigma_x)$, the noise law: supplement pp. A1 and A3, standing assumptions. The averaged target in (iii) is the average of conditional sampling variances, not the variance of $\hat\mu_{HT}$ over both the errors and the sample.

The supplement does not state that the errors are independent across units; zero cross-covariances are what the identity uses. canonical_claim.statement:
Exact witness (validator's construction; not in the paper): a size vector in the support of the stated size law for which the printed first-order ‘inclusion probability’ exceeds one.
Witness. $N = 8$, $m = 2$ (the first configuration of Table A2) and $x = (30, 1, 1, 1, 1, 1, 1, 1)$, so $\sum_l x_l = 37$.
(C1) The printed formula gives $(\pi_1, \ldots, \pi_8) = (60/37, 2/37, 2/37, 2/37, 2/37, 2/37, 2/37, 2/37)$; these sum to $2$ and $\pi_1 - 1 = 23/37 > 0$.
(C2) For any random variable $I_1$ with values in $\{0, 1\}$, $\mathrm{E}(I_1) \le 1$. Hence no sampling design in the paper's sense (main p. 233: $I_k \in \{0,1\}$, $\mathrm{E}(I_k) = \pi_k$) has these first-order inclusion probabilities.
(C3) [The vector has positive probability.] Read the size law as $x_k = 1 + Y_k$ with $Y_1, \ldots, Y_N$ independent negative binomial counts with mean 6 and variance 16, that is $\Pr(Y = j) = \frac{(r)_j}{j!}p^r(1-p)^j$ for $j = 0, 1, 2, \ldots$, with $(r)_j = \prod_{i=0}^{j-1}(r + i)$, $p = 3/8$ and $r = 18/5$ (the solution of $r(1-p)/p = 6$, $r(1-p)/p^2 = 16$). Then $\Pr\big(x = (30, 1, \ldots, 1)\big) = \Pr(Y = 29)\Pr(Y = 0)^7 > 0$.
(C4) [Every configuration of Table A2.] For each $(N, m) \in \{(8,2), (40,2), (120,30), (600,30), (240,60), (1200,60)\}$, with $L = \lfloor (N-1)/(m-1)\rfloor + 1$ (namely $8, 40, 5, 21, 5, 21$), the vector $x = (L, 1, \ldots, 1)$ gives $\pi_1 = mL/(L + N - 1) > 1$ (namely $16/15$, $80/79$, $150/124$, $630/620$, $300/244$, $1260/1220$).
What the witness contradicts: that the display defines first-order inclusion probabilities of a fixed-size design for every size vector the stated law can produce.
canonical_claim.definitions_needed: $I_k$, $\pi_k$: main p. 233 (PDF p. 5), standing assumptions. The size law (‘a vector of $N$ random draws from a negative binomial distribution with mean 6, variance 16, and offset of 1 to avoid zero values’), the display for $\pi_k$ and ‘$m$ is the size of the systematic sample’: supplement p. A3, standing assumptions. The supplement states no certainty-unit rule, redraw or truncation. The reading of ‘mean 6, variance 16’ as moments before the offset is the validator's; under the other reading the support is still unbounded and (C1), (C2), (C4) are unchanged.

canonical_claim.name_in_paper: Supplement Section C, the display for the first-order inclusion probability under systematic PPS sampling, corrected: the feasibility condition $m\max_k x_k \le \sum_l x_l$, or certainty-unit redistribution $\pi_k = \min(1, c\,x_k)$ with $\sum_k\pi_k = m$
canonical_claim.location: Supplement p. A3 (staged/supplements/smj_suppl.pdf, PDF p. 3), Section C: the sentence on the size variable and the display for $\pi_k$
canonical_claim.statement:
Sol's repair (validated.json, P027-E002, smallest_repair), verbatim: "To retain the displayed formula, state that full size vectors are redrawn until m*max_k x_k <= sum_l x_l, and report that conditional size-generation law. Alternatively retain the unconditional size law, replace the display by pi_k=min(1,c*x_k) with sum_k pi_k=m, specify the systematic design using those probabilities, and compute its corresponding joint probabilities. The actual code, if recovered, should determine which description correctly matches the reported runs."
Mathematical content, with every hypothesis (validator's derivation.md, sections ‘Exact counterexample’ and ‘Natural reading, smallest repair, and its cost’).
Setting. $N \ge 2$ units with sizes $x_k > 0$ and an integer $m$ with $0 < m < N$.
(i) [Necessity.] If some sampling design on $\{1, \ldots, N\}$ (indicators $I_k \in \{0, 1\}$) has $\mathrm{E}(I_k) = m x_k/\sum_l x_l$ for every $k$, then $m\max_k x_k \le \sum_l x_l$.
(ii) [Existence of the redistributed probabilities.] There is a real $c > 0$ with $\sum_{k=1}^{N}\min(1, c\,x_k) = m$. (The map $c \mapsto \sum_k\min(1, c\,x_k)$ is continuous and nondecreasing, equals $0$ at $c = 0$ and $N$ for large $c$.) If $m\max_k x_k \le \sum_l x_l$, then $c = m/\sum_l x_l$ works and $\min(1, c\,x_k) = m x_k/\sum_l x_l$: the printed formula.
(iii) [A fixed-size design with given first-order probabilities.] Let $\pi_1, \ldots, \pi_N \in (0, 1]$ with $\sum_k\pi_k = m$. Lay intervals of lengths $\pi_1, \ldots, \pi_N$ end to end on $[0, m)$ (unit $k$ occupies $[\sum_{a<k}\pi_a, \sum_{a \le k}\pi_a)$), draw $u$ uniformly on $[0, 1)$, and select the units whose intervals contain $u, u + 1, \ldots, u + m - 1$. Then every sample has exactly $m$ distinct units and $\mathrm{E}(I_k) = \pi_k$ for every $k$. In particular, when $m\max_k x_k \le \sum_l x_l$ the printed $\pi_k = m x_k/\sum_l x_l$ are the first-order inclusion probabilities of a systematic design of size $m$ (sufficiency, the converse of (i)).
(iv) [The witness of P027-T12, repaired.] For $N = 8$, $m = 2$, $x = (30, 1, 1, 1, 1, 1, 1, 1)$: $c = 1/7$ and $\pi = (1, 1/7, \ldots, 1/7)$. The design of (iii) draws each sample $\{1, j\}$, $j = 2, \ldots, 8$, with probability $1/7$; so $\pi_{1j} = 1/7$ for $j > 1$ and $\pi_{ij} = 0$ for distinct $i, j > 1$. Capping the printed values without redistribution does not give a design of size 2: $\sum_k\min(1, m x_k/\sum_l x_l) = 51/37 \ne 2$.
Corrected recipe: either the size vectors are redrawn until $m\max_k x_k \le \sum_l x_l$ (and the display stands, for that conditional size law), or the display is replaced by $\pi_k = \min(1, c\,x_k)$ with $\sum_k\pi_k = m$ and the joint inclusion probabilities are those of the design that uses these probabilities.
canonical_claim.definitions_needed: $I_k$, $\pi_k$, $\pi_{kl}$: main p. 233, standing assumptions. The size law, the display for $\pi_k$, ‘joint inclusion probabilities are computed as per Madow (1949)’: supplement p. A3. The construction in (iii) is the validator's (it is systematic sampling with the $\pi_k$ as normalized sizes and unit skip); the pairwise probabilities depend on the order of the units, and the first-order probabilities alone do not determine them.
canonical_claim.note: Repair cost recorded by Sol: new_assumption_applications_may_not_satisfy (the formula-preserving repair imposes a feasibility restriction that the stated unconditional size law violates with positive probability; the alternative changes the probability formula and the design on those vectors). Which description matches the reported runs is not known: the code is unavailable. The periodic design of Table A3 is not affected: its largest printed probability is $10m/(6N) \le 5/12$.
